subject: The number most people get wrong
preheader: It's not your salary. Here's how to find the real one in 5 minutes.
goal: Push Day 1 and Day 2 of the reset; build the habit of opening the PDF
html:
Hi,

Quick check: did you do Day 1?

If not, here's the one-minute version, because it's the number everything else depends on.

Most people plan their money around their salary. But you can't spend your salary. You can spend what lands in your account after tax, retirement contributions, health insurance and everything else your payslip quietly removes.

To find your real monthly take-home pay:

  • Paid every two weeks: one paycheck × 26 ÷ 12
  • Paid weekly: one paycheck × 52 ÷ 12
  • Income varies: use your lowest normal month from the last six

Notice it's ×26÷12, not ×2. Paid every two weeks, you get 26 paychecks a year, not 24. Two months a year you get a third paycheck, and if you plan around "two a month" those extra paychecks quietly disappear.

Today is Day 2: the subscription hunt. Search your bank and card statements for "monthly", "renewal", "subscription", and the words "Apple", "Google" and "PayPal". Then ask one question of every charge you find:

If this weren't already running, would I sign up for it today at this price?

If the answer is no, cancel it while you're looking at it. Full walkthrough here: How to find and cancel forgotten subscriptions.

Tomorrow: three free bank alerts that make overdrafts and late fees much less likely.

The Money Made Simple team

subject: Why your last budget died in week three
preheader: It wasn't willpower. It was the design.
goal: Teach the weekly-number idea; first soft mention of the product
html:
Hi,

If you've tried budgeting before and quit, here's something that might help: it probably wasn't you.

Most budgets ask you to manage a dozen categories every single day. Groceries, eating out, fun, household, transport, "misc". Every coffee is a decision. By the third week of the month, the categories that felt huge on the 1st are empty, you can't tell where it went, and opening the spreadsheet just feels bad. So you stop.

Three things make a budget stick instead:

  1. Fewer decisions. One number to watch, not twelve.
  2. A short feedback loop. Weekly, so a bad week is a small problem, not a ruined month.
  3. Automation for everything that doesn't change. Bills and savings move on their own.

That's the idea behind Day 7 of your reset: split your pay into bills, funds, goals and one weekly spending number. The first three run on autopilot. You only watch the fourth.

Example (fictional): Maya takes home $3,050 a month. After bills, funds and goals, she has $832 left for spending. $832 × 12 ÷ 52 = $192 a week. Groceries, takeout, a concert: all of it comes from $192. When it's gone, the week's done.

The full method, with the maths: How to make a budget you'll actually keep.

If you're on schedule, today is Day 3: turn on a low-balance alert, a large-transaction alert, and a payment-due alert on every card. Ten minutes, free, and your accounts start warning you instead of surprising you.

The Money Made Simple team

P.S. I turned this method into a complete guide and spreadsheet called The 20-Minute Budget. More on that in a few days. For now, the free version in your reset is all you need to start.

subject: Car registration isn't an emergency
preheader: The fix for "surprise" expenses that aren't really surprises.
goal: Teach sinking funds; protect the emergency fund they started on Day 4
html:
Hi,

Car registration isn't an emergency. It shows up every single year.

So do holiday gifts, the annual software renewal, the dentist, and the friend's wedding you RSVP'd to in March. They feel like surprises because they're not monthly. And they're the number one reason emergency funds quietly drain: the "emergency" money pays for Christmas, and then the real emergency goes on a credit card.

The fix is a sinking fund: a small monthly amount saved for a cost you know is coming.

Car registration$18012 months$15
Holiday gifts$42012 months$35
New phone$72024 months$30
Dentist + glasses$30012 months$25

Total: $105 a month, one automatic transfer on payday. When the bill arrives, the money's already there, and nothing went wrong.

subject: Avalanche vs snowball: the real difference was $106
preheader: Same debts, same extra payment. Here's what the maths says.
goal: Value on debt payoff; show the spreadsheet's debt planner as a natural fit
html:
Hi,

Avalanche vs snowball gets argued online like a sport. So I ran the actual numbers.

Three hypothetical debts: a $900 store card at 18%, a $4,200 credit card at 27%, and a $6,500 personal loan at 9%. Minimums total $350, plus $200 extra a month.

  • Avalanche (highest rate first): about 25 months, about $1,850 in interest. First debt gone in month 17.
  • Snowball (smallest balance first): about 25 months, about $1,950 in interest. First debt gone in month 5.
  • Minimums only: about 46 months and about $4,300 in interest.

So avalanche saved roughly $106. Snowball delivered the first win a full year sooner.

My take: the best method is the one you're still following in month 12. If rate gaps are big or you're motivated by spreadsheets, avalanche. If you've started and quit before, snowball's small extra cost buys momentum. And either one crushes minimum payments.

One more number that surprises people: a $3,000 card balance at 22% APR, paying $60 a month, takes about 11½ years and costs about $5,200 in interest, more than the balance itself. At $150 a month it's about 26 months and $770.

Full breakdown: Debt avalanche vs snowball, with the real maths.

Want to run your own debts? The debt payoff tab in The 20-Minute Budget compares both methods side by side for up to six debts and gives you a debt-free date.

subject: Paid in full, score still dropped?
preheader: Your card has two dates. Only one of them gets reported.
goal: Pure value on credit; builds trust between pitches
html:
Hi,

Here's a confusing one: you pay your card in full, never pay a cent of interest, and your credit score still dips.

The reason is two dates.

  1. Statement closing date: when the month's statement is generated. The balance on this date is usually what gets reported to the credit bureaus.
  2. Payment due date: usually a few weeks later.

Spend $1,500 on a $2,000 limit and pay it all on the due date, and the bureaus may already have seen 75% utilization. Utilization (how much of your limits you're using) is a big part of the "amounts owed" category, about 30% of a FICO score.

The fix: in a big-spending month, make a payment before the statement closing date. The dip isn't permanent either; once a lower balance is reported, it usually bounces back.

Two more myths while we're here:

  • You don't need to carry a balance to build credit. Paying interest doesn't help your score. Pay in full.
  • Closing an old, no-fee card can hurt. It shrinks your total available credit, so utilization rises. Often better to keep it and use it for one small purchase every few months on autopay.

The whole picture (all five factors, in plain English): How credit scores actually work.

The Money Made Simple team

P.S. If you skipped Day 5 of the reset, the free credit freeze is still worth 15 minutes this week.

subject: $100 a month doesn't sound like investing
preheader: Over 40 years it can quietly become one of the biggest things you own.
goal: Value on investing; move readers toward the next step after budgeting
html:
Hi,

A hundred dollars a month doesn't sound like investing. It sounds like a phone bill.

But as a hypothetical, $100 a month for 40 years at a 7% average annual return grows to roughly $262,000, from $48,000 of contributions. Returns aren't guaranteed and markets go up and down, but starting early gives your money the one thing nobody can buy later: time.

The order that makes sense for most people starting out:

  1. Starter emergency fund (your Day 4 account) so a car repair never forces you to sell investments.
  2. Get your full 401(k) match, if you have one (Day 6). It's often an instant 50–100% on what you put in.
  3. Pay down high-interest debt. Paying off a 22% card is a guaranteed 22% "return".
  4. Then invest more, often in a Roth IRA with a low-cost index fund or a single target-date fund.

Two things beginners get wrong:

  • Depositing isn't investing. Money you add to a brokerage account often lands as cash. You have to actually buy the fund. Check your holdings.
  • Fees compound too. On a $10,000 investment over 30 years (hypothetical 7%), a 1% fee leaves you about $18,000 less than a 0.03% fee. Here's how to check any fund's fee in a minute.

The complete walkthrough, every step: How to start investing with $100 a month.

Roth or Traditional? It mostly comes down to one question.

The Money Made Simple team

P.S. Step 3 is where a lot of people get stuck. Finding the extra money for it is exactly what the weekly-number budget is for.

subject: Will a spreadsheet actually work for me?
preheader: Honest answers to the questions people ask before buying.
goal: Answer objections for The 20-Minute Budget; second pitch
html:
Hi,

Here are straight answers to the questions people usually have before buying a budgeting template like The 20-Minute Budget.

"I've quit every budget I've tried." That's who it's designed for. You don't track categories. You check one weekly number for 20 minutes a week. The guide covers what to do after a bad week, because there will be bad weeks.

"I'm paid every two weeks / my income changes." The Setup tab converts weekly, biweekly or twice-monthly pay. The guide has a section on irregular income: budget from your lowest normal month and use a buffer fund in good months.

"I don't have Excel." It works in Google Sheets (free) and Apple Numbers.

"Does it connect to my bank?" No, on purpose. Nothing to sync, nothing to break, no account access. If you want automatic syncing, a budgeting app is the better choice, and I'd rather you buy the right tool.

"I'm in debt. Is this the right first step?" The debt payoff tab plans up to six debts with avalanche or snowball and shows your debt-free date. If minimum payments themselves feel unmanageable, a nonprofit credit counsellor (an NFCC member agency in the US) is a good next step, and it's often free or low-cost.

"What if it's not for me?" Email within 14 days and you get a full refund.

It's $12, one payment, files you keep.

preheader: Your next three money moves, and what to expect from me from now on.
goal: Recap, last mention of the product (no fake urgency), move to the weekly newsletter
html:
Hi,

Three weeks ago you downloaded the 7-Day Money Reset. Whether you did all seven days or just one, here's where things stand and what comes next.

If you did the reset, your next three moves, in a common order:

  1. Keep your weekly check-in. 20 minutes, same day each week. This is the habit that makes everything else work.
  2. Pick a debt method and point your extra money at one target. Avalanche or snowball.
  3. Grow the emergency fund from $1,000 toward 3–6 months of essential expenses, then start investing.

If life got in the way, start with Day 1 tonight. The PDF is here. Fifteen minutes is enough.

From now on: one email a week, each with a single money move you can make that week, explained with the numbers. If that's not for you, the unsubscribe link is at the bottom, no hard feelings.
